tweets.text:
#uranium #copper #silver #gold

⚡ THE SUNDAY METALS PULSE — 30 AUGUST 2026 ⚡

Four metals. One pulse. No noise.

Friday ended with a serious macro shock.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh struck a distinctly hawkish tone at Jackson Hole, sending the dollar and Treasury yields sharply higher. Markets lifted the probability of a September rate hike from roughly 35% to the mid-50s.

Gold fell 3.2%.
Silver fell 4.3%.
The U.S. 2-year yield jumped to around 4.36%, while the dollar recorded its strongest daily gain in roughly 2½ months.

But this week's move may ultimately be decided by something else entirely:

🇺🇸 THE U.S. LABOR MARKET.

Friday brings the final payroll report before September's Fed decision, and after July unexpectedly LOST 23,000 jobs, expectations remain very subdued. Reuters' weekend preview points to roughly 45,000 new jobs in August.

A weak number could quickly reverse Friday's dollar/yield move.

A strong number could reinforce the hawkish Fed reset.

Here's where my four metals stand.

☢️ URANIUM

Uranium equities cooled into the weekend, but I see little change in the underlying fuel-market thesis.

One important supply issue remains Kazatomprom. Its new TQZ sulphuric-acid plant has been delayed by an estimated 6–12 months and is now expected between Q3 2027 and Q1 2028.

Kazatomprom says there should be no material immediate production impact, but its 2026 production guidance remains explicitly dependent on sulphuric-acid availability.

Meanwhile nuclear buildout continues while new uranium production remains slow, capital intensive and difficult to bring online.

For uranium next week, I will watch whether the recent equity weakness attracts buyers and whether the spot market can regain momentum.

⚡ COPPER

Copper remains perhaps the most interesting industrial metal setup.

LME copper recently reached approximately $14,343/t, just below its $14,527.50 record.

But underneath the headline price there is a major distortion developing.

U.S. copper inventories have surged as traders move metal into America ahead of potential 2027 tariffs, while large withdrawal orders have tightened availability on the LME.

COMEX stocks have climbed to a record ~675,000 tonnes.

This doesn't necessarily mean the world is physically short of copper today.

It means copper is increasingly being stored in the wrong places.

And alongside mine disruptions, Indonesian smelter problems and steadily increasing electricity/grid demand, that creates the potential for violent regional squeezes.

The first major test next week comes from China.

Economists expect China's official manufacturing PMI to remain below 50 in August, around 49.6, indicating a second consecutive month of contraction.

A stronger-than-expected Chinese PMI would be particularly supportive for copper.

🥈 SILVER

Silver suffered most from Friday's macro shock, falling about 4.3%.

But I see virtually no deterioration in the physical thesis.

The Silver Institute still expects the market to record its SIXTH consecutive annual deficit in 2026, with the latest estimate around 46.3 Moz.

Mine production remains essentially stagnant as grade deterioration and operational problems offset growth elsewhere.

And something potentially important is happening in India.

After six months with virtually no silver entering through the India International Bullion Exchange, about 89.8 tonnes have arrived in August. Around 400 tonnes of import licences have reportedly been approved, while customs and documentation bottlenecks continue restricting flows.

With India's festival and wedding season approaching, this deserves attention.

Western investment demand also remains significant. SLV held approximately 15,346 tonnes of silver as of August 27, compared with 15,295 tonnes on August 21.

Silver next week may initially trade as a leveraged bet on gold and Fed expectations.

But underneath that volatility, the physical deficit remains.

🥇 GOLD

Gold's Friday decline was almost entirely macro-driven.

Higher yields.
Stronger dollar.
More Fed tightening priced in.

But the longer-term monetary backdrop is becoming increasingly interesting.
U.S. long-duration borrowing costs remain elevated, the 30-year Treasury yield recently reached 5.327%, and Treasury intervention through expanded bond buybacks is triggering increasingly open discussion about fiscal sustainability and the dollar.
Citigroup's global macro team reportedly continues to favor gold while maintaining a bearish dollar position.

And this weekend the G20 enters the picture.

Finance ministers and central bankers are gathering with U.S. deficits, tariffs, China, Iran, bond-market instability and currency policy all on the agenda.

⚡ THE SUNDAY METALS PULSE — 30 AUGUST 2026 ⚡

Four metals. One pulse. No noise.

Friday ended with a serious macro shock.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh struck a distinctly hawkish tone at Jackson Hole, sending the dollar and Treasury yields sharply higher. Markets lifted the probability of a September rate hike from roughly 35% to the mid-50s.

Gold fell 3.2%.
Silver fell 4.3%.
The U.S. 2-year yield jumped to around 4.36%, while the dollar recorded its strongest daily gain in roughly 2½ months.

But this week's move may ultimately be decided by something else entirely:

🇺🇸 THE U.S. LABOR MARKET.

Friday brings the final payroll report before September's Fed decision, and after July unexpectedly LOST 23,000 jobs, expectations remain very subdued. Reuters' weekend preview points to roughly 45,000 new jobs in August.

A weak number could quickly reverse Friday's dollar/yield move.

A strong number could reinforce the hawkish Fed reset.

Here's where my four metals stand.

☢️ URANIUM

Uranium equities cooled into the weekend, but I see little change in the underlying fuel-market thesis.

One important supply issue remains Kazatomprom. Its new TQZ sulphuric-acid plant has been delayed by an estimated 6–12 months and is now expected between Q3 2027 and Q1 2028.

Kazatomprom says there should be no material immediate production impact, but its 2026 production guidance remains explicitly dependent on sulphuric-acid availability.

Meanwhile nuclear buildout continues while new uranium production remains slow, capital intensive and difficult to bring online.

For uranium next week, I will watch whether the recent equity weakness attracts buyers and whether the spot market can regain momentum.

⚡ COPPER

Copper remains perhaps the most interesting industrial metal setup.

LME copper recently reached approximately $14,343/t, just below its $14,527.50 record.

But underneath the headline price there is a major distortion developing.

U.S. copper inventories have surged as traders move metal into America ahead of potential 2027 tariffs, while large withdrawal orders have tightened availability on the LME.

COMEX stocks have climbed to a record ~675,000 tonnes.

This doesn't necessarily mean the world is physically short of copper today.

It means copper is increasingly being stored in the wrong places.

And alongside mine disruptions, Indonesian smelter problems and steadily increasing electricity/grid demand, that creates the potential for violent regional squeezes.

The first major test next week comes from China.

Economists expect China's official manufacturing PMI to remain below 50 in August, around 49.6, indicating a second consecutive month of contraction.

A stronger-than-expected Chinese PMI would be particularly supportive for copper.

🥈 SILVER

Silver suffered most from Friday's macro shock, falling about 4.3%.

But I see virtually no deterioration in the physical thesis.

The Silver Institute still expects the market to record its SIXTH consecutive annual deficit in 2026, with the latest estimate around 46.3 Moz.

Mine production remains essentially stagnant as grade deterioration and operational problems offset growth elsewhere.

And something potentially important is happening in India.

After six months with virtually no silver entering through the India International Bullion Exchange, about 89.8 tonnes have arrived in August. Around 400 tonnes of import licences have reportedly been approved, while customs and documentation bottlenecks continue restricting flows.

With India's festival and wedding season approaching, this deserves attention.

Western investment demand also remains significant. SLV held approximately 15,346 tonnes of silver as of August 27, compared with 15,295 tonnes on August 21.

Silver next week may initially trade as a leveraged bet on gold and Fed expectations.

But underneath that volatility, the physical deficit remains.

Gold's Friday decline was almost entirely macro-driven.

Higher yields.
Stronger dollar.
More Fed tightening priced in.

Ever wonder why the Big Short legends like Michael Burry and Steve Eisman are now selling subscriptions?

Why so many legendary investors became star guests on CNBC: Bill Gross, Jeremy Grantham, Jim Chanos, Carl Icahn, Bill Miller, Mohamed El-Erian.

Why Paul Tudor Jones, who reportedly once tried to keep old footage of himself trading out of circulation, is now a regular market commentator.

It would also be fascinating to follow every investor who appeared in Market Wizards and see where they are today.

I suspect the full stories would look much less magical.

MAYBE a couple would prove to be genuinely exceptional. But most probably found one great wave, rode it brilliantly for one cycle, then spent years underperforming the index until they quietly disappeared.

Markets are very good at turning luck into genius during the right cycle.

There is no such thing as a permanent edge.
What worked for five, ten, or even twenty years can stop working.

The real test is not whether you had an edge once. It is whether you can keep adapting after it disappears.

David Friedberg: Higher Interest Rates Are About to Make America’s $40 Trillion Debt Problem Much Worse

“The federal government has a problem because over the next 12 months they have to refinance $10 trillion of debt.

That debt is coming due. Those bonds are now due. They have to pay the principal back to the bond holders, and they have to go back to the treasury market and sell more treasuries to borrow more money to refinance.

So the borrowing cost now is going to climb up, and when that borrowing cost climbs up, the federal government's burn goes up and the fiscal deficit goes up.

So my theory and my argument on this is: There is no action that Bessent can take that's actually going to have a meaningful effect on the long end of the curve.

We have a fundamental fiscal spending problem with the federal government right now.

It is very expensive now to borrow money if you're the US federal government. And the reason is persistent inflation, I would argue because of excess government spending on social programs and other things.

And the big problem at this point is the federal government is spending so much that if they were to cut spending aggressively, the argument and the concern is it would hit unemployment and it would cause a recession because the federal government is such an intricate part of the economy now.

That's the argument. But it's causing inflation, and it's causing deficit spending.

So this year the deficit will be roughly $2 trillion. And as a result, the market is saying, ‘We're worried about the US fiscal solvency over the long run, or there's a higher risk. As a result, we're going to charge you a higher interest, 5.2% on the 30 year.’

What does this mean for the federal government?

Well, today, the federal government's average cost of debt is 3.4%. That's what we're paying on interest on average on the $40 trillion of debt that the federal government has outstanding.

For every 1% change in the interest rate, the US government has to pay 1.25% of GDP in excess interest each year. 1.25% of GDP in interest each year for that 1% change in the interest rate.”
